title: The poisoned arrow
hook: a wounded man refuses treatment until he knows who shot him and why (MN 63)

segments.voice: Yesterday: simsapa, the handful of leaves. The Buddha taught only what helps. Your line: only what helps.

A monk named Malunkyaputta is sitting alone, and he's annoyed. There are questions the Buddha has never answered. Is the world eternal, or not? Is it infinite, or finite? Is the soul the same as the body, or different? Does an awakened one exist after death, or not, or both, or neither? He makes up his mind: he'll demand answers, and if the Buddha won't give them, he'll give up the robe and go back to ordinary life. It's an ultimatum. The Buddha answers it with a story about an arrow.
screen: `A MONK, ANNOYED.` → `TEN BIG QUESTIONS.` → `ANSWER, OR I LEAVE.`

segments.voice: First, the Buddha asks him: did I ever say, come and live the holy life and I'll answer these for you? No, Malunkyaputta admits. Did you ever say, I'll live it only if you answer? No. Then the story. A man is shot with an arrow thickly smeared with poison. His friends and family rush to bring a surgeon. But the man says: I won't let this arrow be pulled out until I know who shot me. Was he a noble, a priest, a merchant, a worker? What's his name, his clan? Was he tall or short? Dark or golden-skinned? What village is he from? Was the bow a longbow or a crossbow? What was the bowstring made of? The shaft? Which bird's feathers were on it? That man would die, the Buddha says, and still not know. Whether the world is eternal or not, there is still birth, aging, death, sorrow and grief, and their ending is what he teaches. He left those ten questions undeclared because answering them isn't beneficial and doesn't lead to peace and awakening. What he has declared: this is dukkha, its arising, its ending, the way. He doesn't call the questions stupid, or forbid thinking about them. They're just not the urgent thing. And the list of feathers and bowstrings runs long enough that the man's priorities speak for themselves. The arrow is the hurt itself. The questions are everything a person might want settled before dealing with it.
screen: `DID I EVER PROMISE ANSWERS?` · `WHO SHOT ME? WHAT FEATHERS?` · `HE'D DIE STILL ASKING.` · `UNDECLARED, NOT FORBIDDEN.` · then, large: `PULL THE ARROW OUT.`

segments.voice: Notice a question your mind has been circling: why did they say that, what will happen next year, what did that look mean. Ask honestly whether answering it helps with what hurts right now, and if not, set it down for these few minutes. Then turn gently toward the arrow itself, whatever is actually stinging, and simply feel it with care.
Salla, the Pali word for arrow or dart. A wounded man wants every answer before treatment; the urgent thing is the arrow, not the archer.
Your line: pull the arrow out. The archer can wait; the wound can't. That's day three hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers in different schools tell the parable of the poisoned arrow to explain why the Buddha set certain metaphysical questions aside and focused on the four truths.

match.prompt: match the pieces of the arrow story.
pairs: wanted to know about the archer

fork.setup: you've been shot with a poisoned arrow. the surgeon is here. what do you do?
options: let the surgeon pull it out.
first find out who shot you.
first find out what the bowstring was made of.
fork.reveal: the man in the story insists on knowing everything first, and the Buddha says he'd die still not knowing; the arrow comes first.

original.note: Pali salla: a dart or arrow; the Buddha is called sallakatta, the remover of arrows, a surgeon.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha dodged hard questions.
what it means: he set them aside on purpose, because they don't help end suffering, and named what does.

what a scholar hears: MN 63 lists ten avyākata, undeclared points, on the world, the soul and the Tathāgata after death; whether the Buddha held them unanswerable or merely unhelpful is still discussed by scholars.
recall: the grove of the handful of leaves
a door, like body, speech or mind

chat.says: Why wouldn't the Buddha say whether the world is eternal?
options: Answering doesn't lead to peace; like the wounded man, pull the arrow first.
He didn't know the answer, so he quietly changed the subject.
He thought those questions were stupid and forbade thinking about them.
chat.meaning: In MN 63 the Buddha left those questions undeclared because they don't lead to peace and awakening; the poisoned arrow needs pulling out first.

Malunkyaputta.meaning: a monk who demanded answers to ten big questions

dukkha.meaning: suffering, unease, the pain that comes with life

notes: MN 63 paraphrased: confirm the list of ten undeclared points, the details asked about the archer (class, name and clan, height, complexion, home) and the bow, bowstring, shaft and feathers.

Salla / sallakatta: confirm spelling and the epithet's use (e.g. Itivuttaka 100, Sutta Nipata).
